quickAnswer.question: How do I transcribe a medical recording?
quickAnswer.answer: Upload the recording to TranscriptX, paste the link if it's a video lecture, or press Record and dictate. You get an editable transcript with timestamps in seconds. Check drug names, doses and terms against the audio, then copy the text or download it as DOCX, PDF or TXT for your notes or records.

content: Medical transcription turns spoken healthcare content into written text: dictated visit notes, letters and reports, patient and expert interviews for research, lectures, grand rounds and conference talks. The text can then be edited, searched and added to a record or a paper.

Typing up one hour of audio by hand takes about four hours. TranscriptX turns the recording into text in seconds with a speech model trained on medical terminology, including drug names, doses and clinical language, and keeps a timestamp on each paragraph, so you spend your time reviewing instead of typing.

sections.h2: How to Transcribe a Medical Recording

steps.content: Upload the audio or video file from your device, Google Drive, Dropbox or OneDrive, such as a dictation, an interview or a lecture recording. If it's a video online, paste the link. To dictate a note now, press Record.
TranscriptX detects the language and writes out the recording as punctuated paragraphs, each with a timestamp.

steps.h3: Check terms and doses against the audio
steps.content: Play the recording beside the text, correct drug names, doses and terms with Edit, and keep follow-ups in the Notes tab.
Copy the text into your note, letter or research file, or download it as DOCX, PDF or TXT.

sections.h2: Medical Speech to Text and Dictation in Your Browser
content: There is nothing to install. Open this page on a computer or phone, press Record and dictate your note, then stop and get the text on the same page. Keep the page open while you record.
On the Pro plan, Speak live shows the words as you talk, which suits short dictations you want to see straight away. For longer sessions, record first and transcribe the file afterwards.
You can try AI medical transcription free, without an account. If you dictate or transcribe every day, see the Pro plan.

sections.h2: Check These Before You Use a Medical Transcript
intro: In a medical transcript, one wrong word can change care. Speech recognition handles everyday language well; give these a second listen:

items.content: Pairs like Celebrex and Celexa, or hydroxyzine and hydralazine, are easy to mishear. Confirm every medication name.
15 and 50, mg and mcg, "twice daily" and "twice weekly": check each against the audio.
Side and site matter for findings, procedures and imaging. Make sure "left" and "right" are correct.
"No chest pain" and "chest pain" differ by one short word. Listen for "no", "denies" and "not".
Acronyms, lab values, vital signs and patient or clinician names deserve a final check before the text goes anywhere.

sections.h2: Speaker Labels for Clinicians and Patients
content: Interviews and consultations have several voices. On the Pro plan, TranscriptX labels speakers automatically, so you can see who asked and who answered.

Rename each label to a role, such as Clinician, Patient or Interviewer, during your review. On the Free plan, you get timestamped paragraphs without speaker names, which works well for a single dictation.

sections.h2: AI Transcription, Medical Transcription Services or a Medical Scribe?
intro: Each option fits a different need. Pick by what the text is for:

items.content: Seconds to minutes, with a speech model trained on medical vocabulary. Accurate text on clear audio that you review before it goes into a record. Best for dictations, research interviews, lectures and talks.
Costs nothing but time: about four hours per hour of audio. Practical only for very short notes.
Trained transcriptionists, often billed per line or per minute, with turnaround times and agreements for handling patient data.
A person, or an ambient AI scribe connected to the health record, writes the clinical note during the visit. Medical transcription works from a recording; a scribe works in the room.

content: Recordings that identify patients are protected health information in many countries. TranscriptX does not claim HIPAA compliance. If your organization requires a HIPAA-compliant service with a signed Business Associate Agreement, use one that provides it, or remove patient identifiers before you upload.

Get consent before recording a consultation, and follow your organization's policy. Uploaded files are deleted automatically, and your recordings and transcripts are not used to train AI models. You can delete a single transcript, or all your data, at any time from your account. See the Privacy Policy for details.

items.q: Is there a free medical transcription app?
items.a: You can try TranscriptX free in the browser on a computer or phone, without an account. Speaker labels and Speak live are on the Pro plan.

items.q: How accurate is AI with medical terminology?
items.a: TranscriptX uses a speech model trained on medical terminology, so it recognizes drug names, doses and clinical terms that general speech-to-text often gets wrong. As with any transcript, check doses and rare names against the audio before they go into a patient record.
No. TranscriptX does not claim HIPAA compliance. For recordings with patient identifiers, follow your organization's rules or remove identifiers before uploading.

items.q: Can I dictate notes instead of uploading a file?
items.a: Yes. Press Record on this page and dictate. On Pro, Speak live shows the words as you talk.

items.q: Can it write a SOAP note for me?
items.a: No. TranscriptX gives you the transcript. You can write your SOAP note in the Notes tab beside it, with timestamps linking back to the recording.

items.q: Does it connect to my EHR?
items.a: No. Copy the edited text into your health record, or download it as DOCX, PDF or TXT.
